source: Pfanz (1993): two of Early's brigades reached the crest of East Cemetery Hill at dusk and were driven off.

label: Pickett, Pettigrew and Trimble, about 3 pm; repulsed
source: NPS battle summary, 3 July: after a two-hour cannonade about 12,000 men crossed the open ground to Cemetery Ridge and were repulsed.

label: Lee, 4–5 July
source: NPS battle summary: Lee's army withdrew through Cashtown and Fairfield toward the Potomac from the night of 4 July.

label: I Corps west of the town, XI Corps north of it
source: Coddington (1968), ch. 12: the afternoon line of 1 July, read onto the ridge, the Seminary and the town; approximate.
qc_note: TEST ROW (battle frames): a line of battle.

label: The Union line, 2–3 July
source: NPS battle summary, 2 July: the fishhook from Culp's Hill around Cemetery Hill and down Cemetery Ridge to Little Round Top.
qc_note: TEST ROW (battle frames): a line of battle.

label: The Confederate line, 2–3 July
source: NPS battle summary, 2 July: Ewell through the town, Hill and Longstreet along Seminary Ridge; the line's southern end (Warfield Ridge) has no gazetteer point, so the line stops at the ridge's item; approximate.
qc_note: TEST ROW (battle frames): a line of battle.

label: Taylor 1846
source: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (1974): Taylor marched from Monterrey by Montemorelos and Linares to Victoria, the capital of Tamaulipas, which he reached on 4 January 1847, before Scott drew off most of his regulars.

label: Doniphan 1847
source: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (1974): Doniphan left Chihuahua on 28 April 1847 and marched by Parras, Saltillo and Monterrey to the Rio Grande, where his regiment took ship for New Orleans in June.

label: Santa Anna 1847
source: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (1974): Santa Anna left Mexico City on 2 April 1847 and took up the position at Cerro Gordo on the National Road.

label: Santa Anna 1847
source: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (1974): after Cerro Gordo Santa Anna fell back by Orizaba to Puebla and reached Mexico City on 19 May 1847.

label: El Brazito
source: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (1974): on 25 December 1846 Doniphan's regiment beat off a Mexican force at El Brazito, north of El Paso del Norte. (Placed at the battlefield marker's Wikidata item; the battle has none.)

label: Frémont 1846
source: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (1974); Neal Harlow, California Conquered (1982): Frémont joined the Bear Flag settlers at Sonoma on 25 June 1846 and brought his battalion to Monterey on 19 July.

label: Stockton 1846
source: K. Jack Bauer, Surfboats and Horse Marines: U.S. Naval Operations in the Mexican War, 1846–48 (1969); Harlow (1982): Stockton sailed from Monterey on 1 August 1846 and landed at San Pedro on 6 August; Los Angeles was entered on 13 August.

label: Frémont 1846–47
source: Harlow (1982); K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (1974): the California Battalion marched south from the Monterey country by San Luis Obispo and Santa Barbara and received the Californios' capitulation at Cahuenga on 13 January 1847.

label: Stockton and Kearny 1847
source: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (1974); Harlow (1982): about 600 sailors, marines and dragoons marched from San Diego on 29 December 1846, forced the San Gabriel (8 January 1847), fought at La Mesa (9 January) and re-entered Los Angeles on 10 January.

label: Sonoma seized by American settlers
source: Harlow (1982); K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (1974): on 14 June 1846 settlers took Sonoma and raised the Bear Flag, before news of the war reached California.

label: Monterey taken by the navy
source: K. Jack Bauer, Surfboats and Horse Marines: U.S. Naval Operations in the Mexican War, 1846–48 (1969): Commodore Sloat landed sailors and marines at Monterey on 7 July 1846 and proclaimed California annexed.

label: Los Angeles entered
source: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (1974); Harlow (1982): Stockton and Frémont entered Los Angeles on 13 August 1846.

label: Los Angeles retaken by the Californios
source: Harlow (1982); K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (1974): the Californios under Flores forced Gillespie's garrison to give up Los Angeles on 29 September 1846 and held southern California until January.

label: Dominguez Rancho
source: Harlow (1982); K. Jack Bauer, Surfboats and Horse Marines: U.S. Naval Operations in the Mexican War, 1846–48 (1969): on 8–9 October 1846 the Californios turned back Mervine's landing party marching from San Pedro on Los Angeles.

label: Río San Gabriel
source: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (1974); Harlow (1982): 8 January 1847.

label: La Mesa
source: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (1974); Harlow (1982): 9 January 1847; Los Angeles was re-entered the next day.

label: Capitulation of Cahuenga
source: Harlow (1982); K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (1974): on 13 January 1847 Andrés Pico signed the capitulation with Frémont that ended the fighting in California.

label: Price 1847
source: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (1974): Colonel Sterling Price marched from Santa Fe on 23 January 1847, fought at La Cañada (24 January) and Embudo (29 January) and reached Taos on 3 February.

label: Taos revolt: Governor Bent killed
source: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (1974); National Park Service: on 19 January 1847 New Mexicans and Taos Pueblo people rose against the occupation and killed Governor Charles Bent and other officials at Taos.
qc_note: TEST ROW (review of 2026-11-10). A sensitive event: the revolt, the killings and the executions that followed need the owner's and the co-teachers' words. Not reviewed.

label: La Cañada
source: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (1974): 24 January 1847.

label: Embudo Pass
source: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (1974): 29 January 1847.

label: Siege of Pueblo de Taos
source: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (1974); National Park Service: Price's force stormed the church at Taos Pueblo on 3–4 February 1847, ending the revolt in the north; about 150 defenders were killed.
qc_note: TEST ROW (review of 2026-11-10). Sensitive: see the Taos revolt row. Not reviewed.

label: Conner 1846
source: K. Jack Bauer, Surfboats and Horse Marines: U.S. Naval Operations in the Mexican War, 1846–48 (1969): Conner's squadron sailed from Antón Lizardo and took Tampico, which the Mexican garrison had left, on 14 November 1846.

label: Perry 1847
source: K. Jack Bauer, Surfboats and Horse Marines: U.S. Naval Operations in the Mexican War, 1846–48 (1969): Perry's squadron gathered off Frontera, went up the Grijalva and took San Juan Bautista (Villahermosa), the capital of Tabasco, on 16 June 1847; it was given up on 22 July.

label: Tampico taken by the navy
source: K. Jack Bauer, Surfboats and Horse Marines: U.S. Naval Operations in the Mexican War, 1846–48 (1969): 14 November 1846.

label: Alvarado taken by the navy
source: K. Jack Bauer, Surfboats and Horse Marines: U.S. Naval Operations in the Mexican War, 1846–48 (1969): Alvarado, twice attacked in 1846, surrendered to Lieutenant Hunter on 31 March–1 April 1847.

label: Tuxpan taken by the navy
source: K. Jack Bauer, Surfboats and Horse Marines: U.S. Naval Operations in the Mexican War, 1846–48 (1969): Perry took Tuxpan, the last Gulf port of any size in Mexican hands, on 18 April 1847.

label: Tabasco (San Juan Bautista) taken by the navy
source: K. Jack Bauer, Surfboats and Horse Marines: U.S. Naval Operations in the Mexican War, 1846–48 (1969): 16 June 1847; evacuated 22 July.

label: La Paz taken by the navy
source: K. Jack Bauer, Surfboats and Horse Marines: U.S. Naval Operations in the Mexican War, 1846–48 (1969): the sloop Portsmouth took possession of La Paz, the capital of Baja California, on 14 April 1847.

label: Guaymas taken by the navy
source: K. Jack Bauer, Surfboats and Horse Marines: U.S. Naval Operations in the Mexican War, 1846–48 (1969): Guaymas was bombarded and occupied on 19–20 October 1847.

label: Mazatlán taken by the navy
source: K. Jack Bauer, Surfboats and Horse Marines: U.S. Naval Operations in the Mexican War, 1846–48 (1969): Commodore Shubrick landed at Mazatlán, Mexico's chief Pacific port, on 11 November 1847 and held it until June 1848.

label: Alta California, occupied
source: K. Jack Bauer, Surfboats and Horse Marines: U.S. Naval Operations in the Mexican War, 1846–48 (1969); Harlow (1982): from Sloat's landing at Monterey on 7 July 1846; the south was lost from September 1846 to January 1847 (the province as OpenHistoricalMap draws it, occupied in whole or in part); ceded by the treaty of 2 February 1848.

label: New Mexico, occupied
source: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (1974): from Kearny's entry into Santa Fe on 18 August 1846 (the province as OpenHistoricalMap draws it, occupied in whole or in part); ceded by the treaty of 2 February 1848.

label: Tamaulipas, occupied in part
source: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (1974): Matamoros from 18 May 1846, Camargo, Tampico (14 November 1846) and for a time Victoria (the province as OpenHistoricalMap draws it, occupied in whole or in part); evacuated in the summer of 1848.

label: Nuevo León, occupied
source: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (1974): from the capitulation of Monterrey (24–25 September 1846) (the province as OpenHistoricalMap draws it, occupied in whole or in part); evacuated in June 1848.

label: Coahuila, occupied in part
source: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (1974): Worth entered Saltillo on 16 November 1846; Wool had reached Monclova on 29 October (the province as OpenHistoricalMap draws it, occupied in whole or in part); evacuated in June 1848.

label: Chihuahua, occupied
source: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (1974): Doniphan held the city of Chihuahua from 2 March to 28 April 1847 (the province as OpenHistoricalMap draws it, occupied in whole or in part).

label: Veracruz, occupied in part
source: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (1974): from the surrender of the city on 29 March 1847 (the province as OpenHistoricalMap draws it, occupied in whole or in part); the last troops embarked at Veracruz at the end of July 1848.

label: Puebla, occupied in part
source: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (1974): Worth entered Puebla on 15 May 1847 (the province as OpenHistoricalMap draws it, occupied in whole or in part); evacuated in June 1848.

label: State of Mexico, occupied in part
source: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (1974): Scott's army entered the Valley of Mexico at Ayotla on 11 August 1847; Toluca and Cuernavaca were occupied early in 1848 (the province as OpenHistoricalMap draws it, occupied in whole or in part).

label: Mexico City, occupied
source: K. Jack Bauer, The Mexican War, 1846–1848 (1974): from Scott's entry on 14 September 1847 to 12 June 1848, when the American flag came down in the Zócalo.

label: Baja California, occupied in part
source: K. Jack Bauer, Surfboats and Horse Marines: U.S. Naval Operations in the Mexican War, 1846–48 (1969): La Paz from 14 April 1847 and San José del Cabo from November 1847 (the province as OpenHistoricalMap draws it, occupied in whole or in part); given back by the treaty and evacuated in 1848.
